subsections.html: An enzyme is a protein that speeds up a reaction without being used up. Everything else in this topic follows from one fact: an enzyme works because of its shape. Change the shape and it stops working.

subsections.heading: What an enzyme is
subsections.html:
Spec 2.10

An enzyme is a biological catalyst. "Biological" because it is a protein made by living cells. "Catalyst" because it speeds up a reaction and is not used up.

Every chemical reaction in a living organism — building molecules, breaking them down, respiration — is controlled by enzymes. These are called metabolic reactions. Without enzymes they would happen far too slowly at body temperature to keep you alive.

The two-mark definition of a catalyst

1. A substance that increases the rate of a reaction 1

2. and is not used up / is unchanged at the end 1

"Makes reactions happen" is not enough. The reaction would happen anyway — just slowly.

subsections.heading: The active site and the lock-and-key model
subsections.html:
Spec 2.10

Each enzyme has an active site with a specific shape, and only one substrate fits it.

The substrate is the molecule the enzyme acts on. Its shape is complementary to the active site — it fits the way a key fits a lock. The reaction happens in four steps:

  1. The substrate collides with the enzyme and fits into the active site.
  2. They form an enzyme–substrate complex.
  3. The reaction takes place — the substrate is broken down, or joined to something.
  4. The products are released, and the enzyme is unchanged and ready to be used again.

Because the fit is so exact, each enzyme works on one substrate only. That is called specificity. Amylase cannot digest protein for the same reason a house key will not open a car.

subsections.heading: Temperature, below the optimum — the half everyone forgets
subsections.html:
Spec 2.11 · Y10 2023 Q7 · Y10 2024 Q4

Warming an enzyme up to its optimum makes the reaction faster, because molecules collide more often. Nothing about the enzyme's shape is involved yet.

  1. Higher temperature gives the enzyme and substrate molecules more kinetic energy.
  2. They move faster, so they collide more frequently.
  3. More collisions means more enzyme–substrate complexes form per second.
  4. So the rate of reaction increases.

This is exactly what the snail question wanted, and exactly what students missed. The scheme's marking points were "enzymes · more kinetic energy · more frequent collisions / enzyme substrate complexes form faster · faster respiration".

✗ "The snails at 23 °C are nearer the optimum temperature."
✓ "At higher temperature the enzymes and substrates have more kinetic energy, so they collide more often and more enzyme–substrate complexes form, so respiration and growth are faster."

subsections.heading: Temperature, above the optimum — denaturing
subsections.html:
Spec 2.11

Past the optimum, heat breaks the enzyme's shape, so the substrate no longer fits.

Human enzymes have an optimum of about 37 °C. Above it:

  1. The heat breaks the bonds that hold the protein in its folded shape.
  2. The active site changes shape.
  3. The substrate is no longer complementary to it, so it cannot fit.
  4. No enzyme–substrate complexes form — the enzyme is denatured and the rate falls to zero.

Denaturing is permanent. Cooling a denatured enzyme back down does not fix it, in the same way you cannot un-boil an egg.

✗ "The enzyme dies." — An enzyme is a protein, not a living thing. It cannot die.
✗ "The enzyme changes shape." — Too vague. Say the active site changes shape.
✓ "The active site changes shape, so the substrate no longer fits and the enzyme is denatured."

subsections.heading: Reading a temperature graph
subsections.html:
A rate–temperature graph rises gradually, peaks at the optimum, then falls steeply.

The two sides are not symmetrical, and the difference is worth a mark. The rise is gradual because kinetic energy increases steadily. The fall is steep because once the shape starts breaking, activity collapses quickly.

A question that shows only the rising half — like the snail data, 8 °C to 23 °C — is a kinetic energy question. A question that goes past the peak needs both explanations, one for each side.

subsections.heading: pH — the same ending by a different route
subsections.html:
Spec 2.13

Every enzyme has an optimum pH, and moving away from it in either direction denatures the enzyme.

EnzymeWhere it worksOptimum pH
Salivary amylaseMouthAbout 7
Pepsin (a protease)Stomach — hydrochloric acidAbout 2
Pancreatic enzymesSmall intestine — bile neutralises the acidAbout 8

Too acidic or too alkaline, the charges holding the protein's folds together are disrupted, the active site changes shape, and the substrate no longer fits. Same result as heat, different cause.

Note the direction does not matter. Students often assume only acid is damaging — but putting pepsin into pH 7 denatures it just as surely as putting amylase into pH 2.

subsections.heading: The digestive enzymes
subsections.html:
Spec 2.29 · Y10 2024 Q1(c) · Y11 Jan 2024 Q8(a)

Big food molecules are too large to absorb, so enzymes break them into small soluble ones. The exam wants the named enzyme and the named products.

FoodEnzymeProducts
StarchAmylaseMaltose
MaltoseMaltaseGlucose

The January 2024 mock gave this table with four gaps: amylase, glucose, proteins, fatty acids and glycerol. Every one was a single word worth a mark.

✗ "Amylase breaks starch into glucose." — It skips a stage. Amylase makes maltose; maltase makes glucose.
✗ "Lipase makes fatty acids." — Both products are needed: fatty acids and glycerol.
✗ "Carbohydrase" when the question wants the named enzyme — give amylase.

subsections.heading: Why herbivores need cellulase
subsections.html:
Y11 Jan 2023 Q1(b)

Plant cell walls are made of cellulose, and only an enzyme called cellulase can break it down.

The three-mark chain from the mock scheme:

  1. Plants contain cellulose 1
  2. It is digested by cellulase 1
  3. into glucose, which releases energy in respiration 1

Humans do not make cellulase, so cellulose passes through us undigested as fibre. Specificity again: no enzyme with the right active site, no digestion.

subsections.heading: The iodine test — how every enzyme practical is measured
subsections.html:
Spec 2.12, 2.14B

Iodine turns blue-black when starch is present and stays orange-brown when it is gone. So it tells you when amylase has finished.

  1. Put single drops of iodine in the wells of a spotting tile.
  2. Mix amylase and starch solution in a test tube, in a water bath at a set temperature, and start a stopwatch.
  3. Every 10 seconds, move one drop of the mixture into a new well of iodine.
  4. While starch is present, the iodine turns blue-black.
  5. Record the time when the iodine stays orange-brown — all the starch has been digested.
  6. Repeat at other temperatures, or with buffer solutions of different pH.

A shorter time means a faster reaction. Rate and time go in opposite directions: rate ∝ 1 ÷ time. That is why a graph of time against pH is a valley, while a graph of rate against pH is a peak. Check which is on the axis before describing the shape.

subsections.heading: Designing an enzyme investigation — six marks
subsections.html:
Y11 Jan 2024 Q8(b) — effect of vinegar on starch digestion

Six-mark "design an investigation" questions are marked against a fixed checklist, so write to the checklist. This school uses CORMMSS:

CORMMSS — one mark each

C — Change: what you vary, with a range. "Use different concentrations of vinegar, and no vinegar." 1

O — Organism / object: same material each time. "Same mass of starch." 1

R — Repeat: "Repeat three times at each concentration and calculate a mean." 1

M1 — Measure what: "Test samples with iodine to see if starch remains." 1

M2 — Measure how: "Record the time until the iodine stays orange-brown." 1

S — Same: two controlled variables. "Same temperature using a water bath; same volume and concentration of amylase." 1

"Keep everything else the same" scores nothing. Every control variable must be named.

subsections.heading: When the rate levels off without denaturing
subsections.html:
A reaction can slow and stop even at the perfect temperature and pH. Two reasons, neither of which is denaturing:

  • The substrate is used up — nothing left to bind.
  • All the active sites are occupied — the enzyme is working flat out. Adding more substrate does nothing; adding more enzyme would speed it up.

If the question says conditions did not change, do not reach for "denatured".

The chain behind every mark

Below the optimum: more kinetic energy → more frequent collisions → more enzyme–substrate complexes → faster.

Above the optimum, or wrong pH: active site changes shape → substrate no longer fits → denatured → stops.

questions.promptHtml: Snails grow faster at 23 °C than at 8 °C. A student writes "because 23 °C is closer to the enzymes' optimum." The teacher gives 1 of 3. What was missing?
questions.answerHtml:
The student described where 23 °C sits, not why that speeds things up.

The explanation below the optimum is about kinetic energy. At 23 °C the enzyme and substrate molecules move faster, so they collide more frequently, more enzyme–substrate complexes form, and reactions such as respiration run faster — so the snails grow more.

The test question: would the student's answer have scored better at 45 °C? No — there the snails would grow less, because the enzymes denature. "Closer to the optimum" never explains anything by itself.

questions.promptHtml: An enzyme is heated to 70 °C for five minutes, then cooled back to 37 °C. Does it start working again? Explain.
questions.answerHtml:
No. At 70 °C the bonds holding the protein's shape broke, so the active site changed shape and the enzyme was denatured.

Denaturing is permanent. Cooling does not re-fold the protein into its original shape, so the substrate still does not fit.

The contrast worth knowing: an enzyme cooled to 5 °C does recover when warmed. Cold only slows the molecules down — it never changes the shape.

questions.promptHtml: Pepsin works in the stomach at pH 2. When food moves into the small intestine, pepsin stops working. Why, and why does that not matter?
questions.answerHtml:
Why it stops: bile neutralises the stomach acid, so the pH rises to about 8. That is far from pepsin's optimum, so its active site changes shape and it is denatured.

Why it does not matter: the pancreas releases its own proteases into the small intestine, and their optimum is alkaline. Protein digestion simply carries on with a different enzyme suited to the new pH.

questions.promptHtml: In a pH practical the iodine stays orange-brown after 40 s at pH 6, 20 s at pH 7 and 55 s at pH 8. Which pH is fastest, and why is the shortest time the fastest rate?
questions.answerHtml:
pH 7 — the shortest time.

The iodine stops going blue-black at the moment all the starch has been digested. Getting there in 20 s means the amylase worked twice as fast as at pH 6. Time and rate are inversely related.

Plot time on the y-axis and you get a valley with its lowest point at the optimum. Plot rate and you get a peak. Always read the axis label before describing the shape.

questions.promptHtml: Why can one enzyme not digest starch, protein and fat?
questions.answerHtml:
Because of specificity. The active site has one particular shape, and only a substrate with a complementary shape can fit and form an enzyme–substrate complex.

Starch, protein and lipid molecules all have different shapes, so each needs its own enzyme — amylase, protease and lipase.

questions.promptHtml: A reaction slows and stops, although the temperature and pH have not changed. Give two possible reasons — neither of them denaturing.
questions.answerHtml:
1. The substrate has run out. Nothing is left to bind, so no more product forms.

2. Every active site is occupied. The enzyme is saturated. More substrate would change nothing; more enzyme would speed it up.

How to tell them apart: add more substrate. If the reaction restarts, it had run out. If nothing happens, the enzyme was the limit.

questions.promptHtml: Humans eat plenty of plants but cannot release energy from the cellulose in them. Cows can. Explain the difference.
questions.answerHtml:
Cellulose can only be broken down by the enzyme cellulase, because only cellulase has an active site complementary to it.

Humans do not produce cellulase, so cellulose passes through undigested. Cows have microorganisms in their gut that make cellulase, which digests the cellulose into glucose. The glucose is absorbed and used in respiration to release energy.

questions.promptHtml: Why is the enzyme–temperature graph steeper on the right of the peak than on the left?
questions.answerHtml:
The two sides have different causes.

Left side: kinetic energy increases steadily with temperature, so collision frequency rises gradually and so does the rate.

Right side: once the temperature passes the optimum, bonds holding the protein's shape start breaking and more and more enzyme molecules denature at once. Activity collapses quickly — hence the steep drop.

modules.title: Photosynthesis and Gas Exchange in Plants
modules.standfirst: The biggest single block on the Year 10 checklist — thirteen spec points, two practicals and the limiting-factor graph that turns up in some form almost every year.

subsections.html: Photosynthesis makes glucose out of carbon dioxide and water, using light trapped by chlorophyll inside chloroplasts. It is an endothermic reaction: light energy goes in and is stored as chemical energy.

subsections.heading: The two equations
subsections.html:
Spec 2.18, 2.19

Word equation:

Photosynthesis — word equationcarbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygenlight energy, absorbed by chlorophyll · write "light" and "chlorophyll" above the arrow, not as reactants
Photosynthesis — balanced symbol equation6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂the balancing numbers are a mark of their own · C₆H₁₂O₆ is glucose

Light and chlorophyll are not reactants. Putting them on the left of the arrow is a standard way to lose the mark — they belong above it.

subsections.heading: Limiting factors, and why the graph flattens
subsections.html:
Spec 2.20

Three things can limit the rate: light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature. A limiting factor is the one in shortest supply — the one holding the rate back.

The classic graph rises then levels off. The answer has two halves:

  • On the slope: the factor on the x-axis is limiting. Increase it and the rate increases.
  • On the plateau: that factor is no longer limiting. Something else now is — and the exam wants you to name a plausible candidate, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature.

Temperature behaves differently from the other two, because photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes. Raise it and the rate climbs to an optimum, then falls as the enzymes denature. Light and CO₂ have no such collapse — they simply stop helping.

subsections.heading: Light intensity and the inverse square law
subsections.html:
Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the lamp. Move the lamp from 10 cm to 20 cm and the intensity does not halve — it drops to a quarter.

Light intensity and distancelight intensity ∝ 1 ÷ distance²double the distance → quarter the intensity · treble it → a ninth

subsections.html:

subsections.heading: Gas exchange in plants — the bit students get backwards
subsections.html:
Spec 2.40B, 2.41B, 2.43B, 2.44B

Plants respire all the time, day and night. They photosynthesise only in light. What changes through the day is the net movement of gas, and that word is where the marks are.

ConditionsWhat is happeningNet gas exchange
DarknessRespiration onlyNet O₂ in, net CO₂ out
Dim light (compensation point)Both, at equal ratesNo net exchange
Bright lightPhotosynthesis faster than respirationNet CO₂ in, net O₂ out

Saying "plants respire at night and photosynthesise in the day" is the error the spec point is written to catch. Respiration never stops.

subsections.html:

subsections.heading: The practicals
subsections.html:
Spec 2.23, 2.45B

Oxygen production: pondweed such as Elodea in water with sodium hydrogencarbonate (the CO₂ supply), a lamp at measured distances, and you count bubbles per minute. Use an LED lamp so the water is not heated — otherwise temperature is not controlled.

Testing a leaf for starch: boil in water to kill it, boil in ethanol to remove the chlorophyll, rinse in hot water to soften, then add iodine. Blue-black means starch, so photosynthesis happened. The ethanol must be heated in a water bath, never over a flame — it is flammable.

The three controls each use the same test with one thing removed: cover half a leaf with foil (no light), use a variegated leaf (no chlorophyll in the white parts), or seal the plant with soda lime (no CO₂). In every case the deprived region stays orange-brown.

Hydrogencarbonate indicator measures net gas exchange from a leaf: it is orange at normal CO₂ levels, turns yellow when CO₂ rises (respiration winning) and purple/magenta when CO₂ falls (photosynthesis winning).

The plateau answer, in one line

Where the graph is rising, the x-axis factor is limiting. Where it is flat, it is not — name another factor that now is. Almost every limiting-factor question is that sentence.

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
PhotosynthesisThe process by which plants make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, using light energy absorbed by chlorophyll
Limiting factorThe factor in shortest supply, which is holding back the rate
ChlorophyllThe green pigment that absorbs light — found inside chloroplasts
ChloroplastThe organelle where photosynthesis happens
StomataPores in the lower epidermis where gas exchange and water loss occur

questions.promptHtml: A graph of photosynthesis rate against light intensity rises steeply, then flattens completely. Explain both parts.
questions.answerHtml:
Rising part: light intensity is the limiting factor. As it increases, more light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll, so the rate of photosynthesis increases.

Flat part: light is no longer limiting — increasing it further has no effect. Another factor is now limiting, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature.

The mark is for naming the other factor. "Something else is limiting" does not score.

questions.promptHtml: A lamp is moved from 10 cm to 30 cm from a pondweed. Bubbles fall from 45 per minute to 5. Is that consistent with the inverse square law?
questions.answerHtml:
Treble the distance → intensity falls to 1 ÷ 3² = 1/9 of its value. One ninth of 45 is 5. So yes — the fall is exactly what the inverse square law predicts, which also suggests light was the limiting factor across that whole range.

Had the count fallen only to 15 (a third), light would not have been the sole limiting factor.

questions.promptHtml: A plant is left in bright light. Hydrogencarbonate indicator around it turns purple. Later, in the dark, it turns yellow. Explain both colours, using the word "net".
questions.answerHtml:
Purple in light: photosynthesis is faster than respiration, so there is a net uptake of carbon dioxide. CO₂ in the tube falls and the indicator goes purple.

Yellow in dark: photosynthesis has stopped but respiration continues, so there is a net release of carbon dioxide. CO₂ rises and the indicator goes yellow.

Note what is not true: the plant did not "start respiring" in the dark. It was respiring the whole time — in the light, photosynthesis was simply using CO₂ faster than respiration produced it.

questions.promptHtml: Why is a variegated leaf used to show that chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis, and what result would you expect?
questions.answerHtml:
A variegated leaf has green parts (with chlorophyll) and white parts (without), on the same leaf — so light, CO₂, temperature and water are all identical for both. The only variable is chlorophyll, which makes it a controlled comparison.

After destarching, light and the iodine test: the green parts turn blue-black (starch made) and the white parts stay orange-brown (no starch). Chlorophyll is therefore required.

questions.promptHtml: A student boils a leaf in ethanol over a naked Bunsen flame. Give one safety problem and one reason the plant should have been destarched first.
questions.answerHtml:
Safety: ethanol is highly flammable and would catch fire over a naked flame. It must be heated in a water bath with the Bunsen turned off.

Destarching: leaving the plant in the dark for 24–48 hours first removes any starch already stored. Without that step, a blue-black result could come from starch made before the experiment, so it would not prove anything about the conditions being tested.

questions.promptHtml: A farmer's greenhouse tomatoes grow poorly with yellow leaves. Suggest which mineral ion is short, and why the symptom follows.
questions.answerHtml:
Magnesium ions. Magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll; without enough of it the plant cannot make the green pigment, so leaves turn yellow.

Less chlorophyll also means less light absorbed, so less photosynthesis, less glucose and poorer growth — which links the symptom to the poor yield.

If the leaves were green but the plant simply small, nitrate would be the better answer: nitrate is needed for amino acids and therefore proteins for growth.

modules.title: Respiration
modules.standfirst: Four equations and one distinction that decides most of the marks: respiration releases energy, it does not make it. Every year someone writes "produces energy" and loses the mark for it.

subsections.html:
Respiration is the release of energy from glucose, in every living cell, all the time. The energy is transferred to ATP, which cells then use for movement, growth, keeping warm and building large molecules.

Two points the spec is fussy about. Energy is released, never created or produced — that is conservation of energy, and the mark schemes reject "produces energy" outright. And respiration is not breathing: breathing is ventilation, a separate thing covered in module 4.

subsections.heading: Aerobic respiration
subsections.html:
Spec 2.34, 2.35, 2.37

Uses oxygen, happens in the mitochondria, and breaks glucose down completely — which is why it releases far more energy per glucose molecule.

Aerobic respiration — word equationglucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + waterenergy released and transferred to ATP · in the mitochondria
Aerobic respiration — balanced symbol equationC₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂Othe reverse of photosynthesis · balancing numbers carry their own mark

Notice it is photosynthesis run backwards. That is worth knowing because it makes both equations one thing to remember rather than two.

subsections.heading: Anaerobic respiration — and why it differs in plants and animals
subsections.html:
Spec 2.36, 2.38

Without oxygen, glucose is broken down incompletely. Much less energy is released, and the products differ between organisms.

Anaerobic respiration in animalsglucose → lactic acidin muscle during hard exercise · no CO₂, no water
Anaerobic respiration in plants and yeastglucose → ethanol + carbon dioxidethis is fermentation · used in brewing and bread-making

The animal equation has one product only. Adding carbon dioxide to it is one of the most common errors in this topic — that belongs to the plant and yeast version.

subsections.heading: Oxygen debt and why you keep panting
subsections.html:
During hard exercise the muscles cannot get oxygen fast enough, so they respire anaerobically as well as aerobically. Lactic acid builds up, causing fatigue and cramp.

When you stop, you keep breathing hard to repay the oxygen debt — the extra oxygen needed to break down the lactic acid that accumulated. That is why breathing rate stays high after the exercise has finished, which is the point of the exercise practical in module 4.

subsections.heading: The practical: respiring seeds
subsections.html:

Germinating seeds in a vacuum flask release heat — the thermometer rises over a day or two. The control is a flask of dead (boiled) seeds, killed and rinsed in disinfectant, whose temperature does not rise.

The disinfectant matters: without it, microorganisms on the dead seeds would respire and warm the flask, which would wreck the comparison. Examiners ask why it is needed.

For carbon dioxide, air is drawn through limewater before and after the seeds. The limewater after the seeds turns milky; the limewater before them does not.

The single most-penalised word in this topic

Respiration releases energy from glucose. It does not produce, create or make energy. Mark schemes in this department explicitly reject "energy production".

questions.promptHtml: A student writes: "Respiration happens in the lungs and produces energy for the body." Give three corrections.
questions.answerHtml:
1. Location. Respiration happens in every living cell (aerobic respiration in the mitochondria), not in the lungs. The lungs do gas exchange.

2. "Produces". Respiration releases energy that was already stored in glucose. Energy cannot be created.

3. What the energy does. It is transferred to ATP, which supplies energy for cell processes — movement, growth, keeping warm, building molecules.

questions.promptHtml: A sprinter's muscles ache after a 200 m race, and they keep breathing heavily for several minutes. Explain both, naming the substance responsible.
questions.answerHtml:
During the race the muscles could not get oxygen fast enough, so they respired anaerobically as well as aerobically. This produced lactic acid, which builds up and causes the ache and fatigue.

Afterwards the sprinter continues to breathe heavily to take in extra oxygen — the oxygen debt — which is used to break down the lactic acid. Once it is cleared, breathing returns to normal.

questions.promptHtml: Why does anaerobic respiration release so much less energy than aerobic respiration from the same amount of glucose?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the glucose is broken down incompletely. Without oxygen the molecule is only partly broken apart, so most of the chemical energy is still locked in the products — lactic acid in animals, ethanol in plants and yeast.

Aerobic respiration breaks glucose down completely to carbon dioxide and water, releasing far more of the stored energy.

Evidence for this: ethanol burns. If anaerobic respiration had extracted all the energy, there would be none left in the product to burn.

questions.promptHtml: In the respiring seeds practical, why must the dead seeds be rinsed in disinfectant, and why is a vacuum flask used?
questions.answerHtml:
Disinfectant: it kills microorganisms on the dead seeds. Those microbes would respire and release heat, so the "dead" flask would warm up too and the control would prove nothing.

Vacuum flask: it insulates, so heat released by respiration is not lost to the surroundings. Without it the temperature rise would be too small to measure.

questions.promptHtml: Yeast is used to make both bread and beer. Explain, using one equation, why the same organism does two apparently different jobs.
questions.answerHtml:
Both rely on anaerobic respiration in yeast: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide.

In bread, the useful product is the carbon dioxide — the bubbles make the dough rise. The ethanol evaporates during baking.

In beer, the useful product is the ethanol, and the carbon dioxide provides the fizz.

One reaction, two different products being harvested.

modules.title: Gas Exchange in Humans
modules.standfirst: Five spec points, and the alveolus adaptation question is worth four of them on its own. Learn the adaptations as a list of feature → why pairs, because that is exactly how the marks are split.

subsections.html: Air travels trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli. The alveoli are where gas exchange happens: oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out. Everything above the alveoli is plumbing.

subsections.heading: The structure of the thorax
subsections.html:
Spec 2.46

StructureWhat it does
TracheaCarries air to the lungs; held open by rings of cartilage
BronchiOne to each lung, branching from the trachea
BronchiolesFine branches ending at the alveoli
AlveoliTiny air sacs — the site of gas exchange
RibsProtect the lungs and move during ventilation

subsections.heading: Ventilation — the two movements
subsections.html:
Spec 2.47

This is a pressure story, and it needs all four steps in order. Volume changes first, pressure follows, air moves last.

Breathing in (inspiration)Breathing out (expiration)
Intercostal musclesContractRelax
RibcageMoves up and outMoves down and in
DiaphragmContracts and flattensRelaxes and domes upwards
Volume of thoraxIncreasesDecreases
Pressure in thoraxDecreases (below atmospheric)Increases (above atmospheric)
AirMoves inMoves out

The diaphragm flattens when it contracts. It is a domed muscle at rest, so contracting pulls it down into a flatter shape — students routinely write that it "moves up" when breathing in, which is exactly backwards.

subsections.heading: How the alveolus is adapted — the four-mark answer
subsections.html:

Each adaptation must be paired with why it speeds diffusion. A bare list of features scores half marks at best.

"Maintains the concentration gradient" is the phrase that separates a 2-mark answer from a 4-mark one. Blood flow keeps oxygen low on the blood side; breathing keeps it high on the air side; the difference is what drives diffusion.

Controls worth naming: same person, same exercise and duration, same rest before starting, and counting over the same time interval.

Muscles contract → volume increases → pressure decreases → air moves in. Reverse every step for breathing out. Never skip the pressure step — it is its own mark.

questions.promptHtml: Explain how air is drawn into the lungs, from muscle contraction to air movement.
questions.answerHtml:
The intercostal muscles contract, pulling the ribcage up and out. At the same time the diaphragm contracts and flattens, moving down.

Together these increase the volume of the thorax. Increasing the volume decreases the pressure inside, so it falls below atmospheric pressure. Air therefore moves in, down the pressure gradient.

The lungs are passive throughout — they do not pull. Answers phrased as "the lungs suck air in" miss the pressure mark, which is the one the question is really testing.

questions.promptHtml: A patient with emphysema has fewer, larger alveoli. Explain why they become breathless during mild exercise.
questions.answerHtml:
Fewer, larger alveoli means a much smaller total surface area for gas exchange. Less oxygen can diffuse into the blood per breath.

During exercise the muscles respire faster and need more oxygen, but the damaged lungs cannot supply it. The patient breathes faster and deeper to compensate, and still feels short of breath. More anaerobic respiration occurs, producing lactic acid and fatigue.

questions.promptHtml: Why does blood flowing past the alveoli keep gas exchange going, rather than diffusion simply stopping once the gases equalise?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the blood is constantly replaced. Deoxygenated blood arriving has a low oxygen concentration, and oxygenated blood carrying oxygen away is removed. This maintains the concentration gradient.

Breathing does the same job on the other side: fresh air keeps the alveolar oxygen concentration high and carbon dioxide low.

If both stopped, the concentrations would equalise and net diffusion would stop — which is exactly what happens if you hold your breath.

questions.promptHtml: A smoker gets repeated chest infections. Explain the link, naming the component of smoke responsible.
questions.answerHtml:
Tar paralyses and destroys the cilia lining the airways.

Normally the cilia sweep mucus — which traps dust, bacteria and other pathogens — up and out of the lungs. With the cilia damaged, that mucus stays in the airways, along with the bacteria trapped in it.

The trapped bacteria multiply, causing repeated infections such as bronchitis. The build-up of mucus also triggers the persistent "smoker's cough".

questions.promptHtml: A student's breathing rate is 14 at rest, 32 immediately after exercise, and still 20 two minutes later. Explain the third figure.
questions.answerHtml:
Breathing rate stays above resting because of the oxygen debt. During exercise some muscle respiration was anaerobic, producing lactic acid.

Extra oxygen is needed to break down that lactic acid, so breathing remains elevated until it has been cleared. Only then does the rate return to 14.

A common wrong answer is "the body is still recovering" — true but not creditworthy. The mark is for naming lactic acid and the oxygen needed to remove it.

modules.title: Heart, Circulation, Blood and Immunity
modules.standfirst: Eleven spec points — the joint largest block on the Year 10 checklist. The double circulatory system, the four blood components and the vessel comparison table between them cover most of what gets asked.

subsections.html: Humans have a double circulatory system: blood passes through the heart twice for every complete circuit of the body. One loop goes to the lungs, the other to the rest of the body.

subsections.heading: Why double beats single
subsections.html:
Spec 2.52

The pulmonary circuit carries blood from the right side of the heart to the lungs and back. The systemic circuit carries it from the left side to the body and back.

The advantage, and the mark: blood is re-pressurised after the lungs. Lung capillaries are delicate, so blood must pass through them slowly at low pressure. Returning it to the heart lets it be pumped out again at high pressure, so it reaches the body quickly. A single circulation would deliver blood to the body slowly, limiting the rate of respiration.

The left ventricle therefore has a much thicker muscular wall than the right: it pumps to the whole body, while the right pumps only to the lungs.

subsections.heading: The heart, chamber by chamber
subsections.html:
Blood arrives in an atrium and leaves from a ventricle. Valves stop it going backwards.

VesselCarries bloodOxygenated?
Vena cavaBody → right atriumDeoxygenated
Pulmonary arteryRight ventricle → lungsDeoxygenated
Pulmonary veinLungs → left atriumOxygenated
AortaLeft ventricle → bodyOxygenated

The pulmonary vessels are the exception to the usual rule. Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry it towards the heart — that is the definition, and it is about direction, not oxygen. The pulmonary artery is the one artery carrying deoxygenated blood.

The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself with oxygen and glucose. If they narrow with fatty deposits, the heart muscle is starved of oxygen — coronary heart disease, and a complete block causes a heart attack.

subsections.heading: The three vessels
subsections.html:
Spec 2.59 – 2.61

ArteryVeinCapillary

Each feature follows from the pressure. Arteries have thick elastic walls to withstand and smooth out high pressure from the heart. Veins have valves because pressure is too low to stop backflow on its own, and a wide lumen to reduce resistance. Capillaries are one cell thick to give a short diffusion distance for exchange with the tissues.

Red blood cells have no nucleus — that is the adaptation examiners most want, because it makes room for more haemoglobin. Saying they "have a nucleus to control the cell" is a guaranteed lost mark.

subsections.heading: Clotting, and why it matters
subsections.html:
Platelets trigger a series of reactions that convert soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin, which forms a mesh trapping red blood cells to make a clot.

Two reasons it matters: it prevents blood loss, and it stops pathogens entering through the wound.

subsections.heading: Immunity
subsections.html:
Spec 2.66, 2.68, 2.69

Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens — non-specific, they attack anything foreign.

Lymphocytes produce antibodies, which are specific: each antibody has a shape complementary to one antigen on the pathogen's surface. Antibodies bind to the antigens, clumping pathogens together so phagocytes destroy them.

Memory cells remain after an infection. On a second exposure they produce antibodies faster and in greater quantity, so the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms appear. That is immunity, and it is how vaccination works: a harmless form of the pathogen is introduced so lymphocytes make antibodies and memory cells without you getting ill.

The rule that survives the pulmonary exception

Arteries carry blood AWAY from the heart; veins carry it TOWARDS the heart. Define them by direction, never by oxygen — otherwise the pulmonary artery and vein look like mistakes.

questions.promptHtml: Explain the advantage of a double circulatory system over a single one, as found in fish.
questions.answerHtml:
In a single circulation, blood passes through the gill capillaries and then straight on to the body. Capillaries are narrow and offer high resistance, so blood leaves them at low pressure and travels slowly to the tissues.

In a double circulation the blood returns to the heart after the lungs and is pumped again at high pressure. It therefore reaches the body tissues much more quickly, so oxygen and glucose are delivered faster and a higher rate of respiration is possible.

That last clause is what makes it an advantage: mammals are warm-blooded and need a high metabolic rate.

questions.promptHtml: A baby is born with a hole between the left and right ventricles. Explain why they tire easily.
questions.answerHtml:
The hole lets oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix in the ventricles.

Blood leaving the left ventricle for the body therefore carries less oxygen than normal. Less oxygen reaches the respiring tissues, so less aerobic respiration occurs and less energy is released.

More anaerobic respiration takes place instead, producing lactic acid, so the baby tires quickly.

questions.promptHtml: Explain why veins need valves but arteries do not.
questions.answerHtml:
Blood in arteries is at high pressure because it has just been pumped from the heart. That pressure alone keeps it moving forwards, so there is nothing to stop.

By the time blood reaches the veins it has passed through the capillaries, and the pressure is low. Without help it could flow backwards, particularly when travelling upwards from the legs against gravity. The valves close if blood starts to move the wrong way, so flow stays one-directional.

Veins also rely on the contraction of nearby skeletal muscles to squeeze blood along.

questions.promptHtml: Why does someone infected with measles a second time usually show no symptoms?
questions.answerHtml:
After the first infection, memory cells specific to the measles antigen remain in the blood.

On the second exposure these memory cells recognise the antigen immediately and produce the specific antibodies much faster and in far greater quantity.

The pathogen is destroyed before it can multiply enough to cause symptoms. This is immunity, and vaccination produces the same state deliberately using a harmless form of the pathogen.

questions.promptHtml: A red blood cell has no nucleus, no mitochondria and a biconcave shape. Explain how each suits its function.
questions.answerHtml:
No nucleus: leaves more room for haemoglobin, so each cell carries more oxygen.

No mitochondria: the cell cannot respire aerobically, so it does not use up any of the oxygen it is carrying — all of it is delivered to the tissues.

Biconcave disc: gives a large surface area to volume ratio for fast diffusion of oxygen in and out, and makes the cell flexible enough to squeeze through narrow capillaries.

The trade-off: with no nucleus the cell cannot repair itself or divide, which is why red blood cells only last about 120 days.

questions.promptHtml: Explain how a blood clot forms, and give two reasons clotting is important.
questions.answerHtml:
Platelets arrive at the wound and trigger a series of reactions that convert soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin. The fibrin forms a mesh of fibres across the wound, trapping red blood cells to form a clot, which dries into a scab.

Why it matters: it prevents further blood loss, and it seals the wound so pathogens cannot enter.

modules.title: Nervous System and the Eye
modules.standfirst: Eleven spec points. The reflex arc must be written in the right order with the right five words, and the two eye reflexes work by opposite pairs of muscles — that pairing is where most marks are lost.

subsections.html: The nervous system detects stimuli and produces responses, using electrical impulses that travel fast. It splits into the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system (all the nerves connecting to it).

subsections.heading: The reflex arc, in order
subsections.html:
Spec 2.86 – 2.88

A reflex action is rapid, automatic and does not involve conscious thought — the brain is not part of the pathway. That speed is protective.

The reflex arc — learn this orderstimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (spinal cord) → motor neurone → effector → responseeffector = muscle or gland · the brain is NOT in the pathway

Every stage carries a mark in a long-answer question. The two words most often missing are relay and effector.

StageIn the hand-on-a-pin example
StimulusThe sharp pin
ReceptorPain receptor in the skin
Sensory neuroneCarries the impulse to the spinal cord
Relay neuroneInside the spinal cord, connects sensory to motor
Motor neuroneCarries the impulse to the muscle
EffectorThe biceps muscle
ResponseThe arm pulls away

equations.formula: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (spinal cord) → motor neurone → effector → response

subsections.heading: The synapse
subsections.html:
Spec 2.89

A synapse is the gap between two neurones. An electrical impulse cannot jump it, so the signal is carried chemically:

  1. The impulse arrives at the end of the first neurone.
  2. It triggers the release of a neurotransmitter into the gap.
  3. The neurotransmitter diffuses across the synapse.
  4. It binds to receptors on the next neurone.
  5. A new electrical impulse is started.

Because the transmitter is released on one side only, synapses make the signal travel in one direction.

Reflex: stimulus → receptor → sensory → relay → motor → effector → response.
Near focus: ciliary contracts → ligaments slacken → lens fatter → more refraction.

questions.promptHtml: Describe the pathway of a reflex when someone treads on a drawing pin, naming every stage.
questions.answerHtml:
The pin is the stimulus. Pain receptors in the skin of the foot detect it and start an electrical impulse.

The impulse travels along a sensory neurone to the spinal cord, where it passes across a synapse to a relay neurone, then across another synapse to a motor neurone.

The motor neurone carries the impulse to the effector — a leg muscle — which contracts. The response is that the foot is lifted away.

Because the pathway goes through the spinal cord and not the brain, it is far quicker, which limits the damage.

questions.promptHtml: You walk from bright sunshine into a dark room and cannot see for a moment. Explain what your iris does, and why.
questions.answerHtml:
In the dark, the radial muscles contract and the circular muscles relax. This dilates the pupil, making it wider.

A wider pupil lets more light enter and reach the retina, so enough light falls on the rod cells to form an image.

The moment of blindness happens because the change is not instant — the muscles take a short time to respond, and the rods need time to adjust to dim light.

questions.promptHtml: Explain how the eye changes focus from a distant hill to a book held close.
questions.answerHtml:
Looking at the hill, the ciliary muscles are relaxed, so the suspensory ligaments are pulled tight and the lens is thin — little refraction is needed for nearly parallel light rays.

Switching to the book, light rays arrive diverging and need bending more. The ciliary muscles contract, which slackens the suspensory ligaments. With the tension released the lens becomes fatter and more curved, refracting light more strongly so it focuses on the retina.

The counter-intuitive part is that contracting a ring of muscle releases tension on the ligaments. The ciliary muscle is a ring: contracting makes the ring smaller, so the ligaments attached around it go slack.

questions.promptHtml: Why can a nerve impulse travel in only one direction across a synapse?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the neurotransmitter is only stored and released on one side — the end of the first neurone — and the receptors that detect it are only on the other side, on the second neurone.

There is nothing to release transmitter travelling backwards and no receptor to receive it, so the signal cannot cross in the opposite direction.

questions.promptHtml: Someone loses colour vision in dim light but sees shapes fine. Which receptor cells are involved, and why does this happen?
questions.answerHtml:
Cones detect colour but need bright light to work. Rods work in dim light but only give black and white.

In dim light there is not enough light to stimulate the cones, so only the rods respond. Shapes and movement are still visible, but without cone stimulation there is no colour information — which is why everything looks grey at night.

modules.title: Hormones and Plant Tropisms
modules.standfirst: Two control systems compared, plus auxin. The nervous-versus-hormonal table is nearly guaranteed, and the auxin explanation needs the words unequal distribution to score.

subsections.html: Animals coordinate responses two ways: nervously, using electrical impulses, and hormonally, using chemicals carried in the blood. Plants use chemicals only.

subsections.heading: Hormones — the definition that earns marks
subsections.html:
Spec 2.79

A hormone is a chemical messenger made in an endocrine gland, carried in the blood, that acts on target organs.

All four elements matter. Students routinely lose a mark by saying hormones travel "around the body" rather than in the blood, or by omitting that they act on specific target organs rather than everything.

subsections.heading: Nervous versus hormonal
subsections.html:
Spec 2.80, 2.81

NervousHormonal

Transmitted byNeuronesThe bloodstream

Speed and duration are the two comparisons worth having ready, and they must be phrased as comparisons: "nervous is faster than hormonal", not "nervous is fast".

subsections.html:

subsections.heading: Adrenaline, explained rather than listed
subsections.html:
Adrenaline is released when you are frightened or stressed. Every effect serves the same purpose: preparing for "fight or flight".

Increased heart rate and increased breathing rate deliver more oxygen and glucose to the muscles, so more respiration can occur and more energy is released for movement. Blood glucose rises to supply that respiration, and pupils dilate to let in more light so you can see more.

Answers that just list the effects get fewer marks than answers that link them to respiration in the muscles.

subsections.heading: Plant tropisms
subsections.html:
Spec 2.93

A tropism is a growth response towards or away from a stimulus. Two to know:

TropismStimulusShootsRoots
PhototropismLightPositive — grow towardsNegative
GravitropismGravityNegative — grow awayPositive — grow down

The advantages: shoots growing towards light get more light for photosynthesis; roots growing down reach water and mineral ions, and anchor the plant.

subsections.heading: Auxin — the mechanism
subsections.html:
Auxin is a plant hormone made at the tip of a shoot. It causes cell elongation — cells get longer.

When light comes from one side, auxin moves to the shaded side. That gives an unequal distribution: more auxin on the shaded side than the lit side. The cells on the shaded side therefore elongate more, so that side grows longer and the shoot bends towards the light.

Three things make this a full-mark answer: auxin made at the tip, it accumulates on the shaded side, and the unequal distribution causes unequal growth. Answers saying the plant "grows towards the light because it wants light" score nothing — plants have no intent, and the mark is for the mechanism.

In roots, auxin has the opposite effect: it inhibits elongation. So the side with more auxin grows less, which is why roots bend downwards rather than up.

The auxin sentence

Auxin is made at the tip → moves to the shaded side → unequal distribution → cells there elongate more → the shoot bends towards the light. Say all five and the marks are yours.

questions.promptHtml: A shoot on a windowsill bends towards the window. Explain fully, in terms of auxin.
questions.answerHtml:
Auxin is produced at the tip of the shoot. Because light is coming from one side, the auxin moves away from the light and accumulates on the shaded side.

This gives an unequal distribution of auxin — a higher concentration on the shaded side than the lit side.

Auxin causes cell elongation, so the cells on the shaded side grow longer than those on the lit side. The shaded side of the shoot therefore becomes longer, and the shoot bends towards the light.

The advantage is that the leaves receive more light, so the plant can photosynthesise more.

questions.promptHtml: Why does a root grow downwards when auxin also collects on its lower side?
questions.answerHtml:
Gravity causes auxin to accumulate on the lower side of the root, just as it collects on the shaded side of a shoot.

The difference is the effect: in roots, auxin inhibits cell elongation rather than promoting it. So the lower side, with more auxin, elongates less than the upper side.

The upper side grows more, so the root bends downwards — positive gravitropism. This takes it towards water and mineral ions, and anchors the plant.

The same hormone, the same distribution, opposite effect. That reversal is the whole point of the question.

questions.promptHtml: A student is startled by a loud bang. Their heart races for several minutes. Explain why the response involves both control systems.
questions.answerHtml:
Nervous: the sound is detected and an impulse travels along neurones to produce the immediate jump or flinch. This is very fast but short-lived.

Hormonal: adrenaline is released from the adrenal glands into the blood. It travels to target organs including the heart, increasing heart rate and breathing rate.

Because the hormone must be carried in the blood, this response is slower to start but lasts much longer — which is why the heart is still racing minutes after the bang, long after the nervous response has finished.

questions.promptHtml: If the tip is cut off a shoot, it stops bending towards light. What does this show?
questions.answerHtml:
It shows that the tip is where auxin is produced. Removing it removes the source of the hormone, so no unequal distribution can build up and no unequal growth occurs — the shoot grows straight.

Covering the tip with an opaque cap gives the same result, showing that the tip is also where the light is detected. Covering the shoot below the tip while leaving the tip exposed still produces bending, which confirms it.

modules.title: Homeostasis, Excretion and the Kidney
modules.standfirst: Nine spec points, and the hardest block on the Year 10 checklist. Filtration then selective reabsorption, negative feedback in both directions, and the ADH loop that students most often get backwards.

subsections.html: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment. Three things are controlled: body temperature, blood glucose and water content. All three work by negative feedback — a change is detected and a response is triggered that reverses it.

subsections.heading: Excretion is not egestion
subsections.html:
Spec 2.71

Excretion is the removal of the waste products of metabolism — substances the body made. Egestion is the removal of undigested food as faeces, which was never absorbed and never part of a reaction.

OrganExcretes
LungsCarbon dioxide (and water vapour)
KidneysUrea, excess water and excess salts
SkinWater, salts and urea in sweat

The liver produces urea but does not excrete it, so it is not the excretory organ for urea — a distinction examiners like.

subsections.heading: Where urea comes from
subsections.html: Excess amino acids cannot be stored. In the liver they are deaminated: the amino group is removed, forming ammonia, which is highly toxic. The ammonia is immediately converted to the less toxic urea, which travels in the blood to the kidneys for excretion.

subsections.heading: The kidney: filtration then selective reabsorption
subsections.html:
Spec 2.72B – 2.75B

This is a two-stage process, and the whole topic depends on keeping them separate.

Stage 1 — ultrafiltration. Blood arrives at the glomerulus under high pressure. Small molecules are forced out into the Bowman's capsule: water, glucose, salts and urea. Large molecules stay in the blood: proteins and blood cells are too big to pass through.

Stage 2 — selective reabsorption. As the filtrate travels along the tubule, useful substances are taken back into the blood:

SubstanceWhat happensHow
GlucoseAll reabsorbedActive transport (against the gradient)
WaterAmount varies with needOsmosis
SaltsAs much as neededActive transport
UreaNot reabsorbedStays in the filtrate and leaves as urine

The word selective is the point: the kidney filters almost everything out, then chooses what to take back. Glucose is reabsorbed by active transport, which requires energy from respiration — that is why kidney tubule cells contain many mitochondria.

The path of urine: kidney → ureter → bladder → urethra. Ureter and urethra are easy to swap, and the mark schemes do not accept the wrong one.

subsections.heading: Water balance and ADH — the loop to get right
subsections.html:
Spec 2.76B – 2.79B

When you are dehydrated — too little water, so blood is too concentrated:

  1. The change is detected (by the brain).
  2. The pituitary gland releases more ADH into the blood.
  3. ADH makes the kidney tubules more permeable to water.
  4. More water is reabsorbed into the blood.
  5. A small volume of concentrated urine is produced, and blood water content rises back to normal.

When you have drunk a lot — blood too dilute — every step reverses: less ADH, tubules less permeable, less water reabsorbed, and a large volume of dilute urine.

The error to avoid: ADH does not "remove water" or "make you urinate more". More ADH means less urine. Reading the name as "anti-diuretic — anti-weeing" fixes the direction permanently.

subsections.heading: Negative feedback, stated generally
subsections.html:
Every homeostatic mechanism has the same shape: a change is detected, a response is triggered that opposes the change, and the level returns towards normal. Because the response opposes the change, the system is self-correcting.

Blood glucose is the other example worth knowing. Insulin lowers blood glucose (causing the liver to convert glucose to glycogen for storage); glucagon raises it (converting glycogen back to glucose). Two hormones, opposite directions, same gland — the pancreas.

The two sentences this topic turns on

Filtration is not selective; reabsorption is. Everything small is forced out, then the useful things are taken back.
More ADH → more water reabsorbed → less urine. Anti-diuretic means anti-urine.

questions.promptHtml: A person runs a marathon on a hot day and drinks very little. Describe what happens to their urine and explain the hormonal control.
questions.answerHtml:
They lose a lot of water in sweat, so the water content of the blood falls and the blood becomes more concentrated.

This is detected, and the pituitary gland releases more ADH into the blood. ADH makes the kidney tubules more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed back into the blood by osmosis.

The result is a small volume of concentrated urine, darker in colour. Blood water content returns towards normal — negative feedback.

questions.promptHtml: Protein is found in a patient's urine. Explain what this suggests about their kidneys.
questions.answerHtml:
Normally protein molecules are too large to be filtered at the glomerulus, so they stay in the blood and never enter the filtrate at all.

Protein in the urine therefore suggests the filtering membrane is damaged — the pores have become too large, letting protein through.

Note the reasoning: this cannot be a reabsorption problem, because protein is never in the filtrate to be reabsorbed. That distinction is what the question is testing.

questions.promptHtml: Why does an untreated diabetic have glucose in their urine, when a healthy person has none?
questions.answerHtml:
In a healthy person, glucose is filtered out at the glomerulus but all of it is reabsorbed by active transport, so none reaches the urine.

In an untreated diabetic, blood glucose is very high because there is too little insulin to lower it. So much glucose is filtered that the active transport system becomes saturated — it cannot reabsorb it all.

The excess glucose stays in the filtrate and appears in the urine.

questions.promptHtml: Explain why kidney tubule cells contain a large number of mitochondria.
questions.answerHtml:
Glucose and salts are reabsorbed by active transport, which moves substances against the concentration gradient.

Active transport requires energy, which is released by aerobic respiration. That happens in the mitochondria, so cells doing a lot of active transport need many of them.

The same reasoning explains why root hair cells in plants are also packed with mitochondria.

questions.promptHtml: Explain why urea must be removed from the body, and where it is made.
questions.answerHtml:
The body cannot store excess amino acids. In the liver they are deaminated — the amino group is removed — producing ammonia, which is highly toxic.

The liver immediately converts ammonia into the less toxic urea. Even so, urea is still a waste product and would be harmful if it built up, so it is carried in the blood to the kidneys and excreted in the urine.

A point worth keeping straight: urea is made in the liver but excreted by the kidneys.

questions.promptHtml: Someone drinks two litres of water quickly. Describe the changes in ADH and in their urine.
questions.answerHtml:
The water content of the blood rises, so the blood becomes too dilute.

The pituitary releases less ADH. The kidney tubules become less permeable to water, so less water is reabsorbed.

More water stays in the filtrate, producing a large volume of dilute, pale urine. Blood water content falls back to normal.

modules.title: Ecology and the Environment
modules.standfirst: Nine spec points, and the only topic on the Year 10 list with a calculation in it. The quadrat estimate and the pyramid of biomass are where the marks concentrate.

subsections.heading: The four terms, in order of size
subsections.html:
Spec 4.1

LevelWhat it covers
HabitatThe place where an organism lives
PopulationAll the organisms of one species in a habitat
CommunityAll the populations of different species in a habitat
EcosystemThe community plus the non-living environment it interacts with

The ecosystem definition needs the non-living part — water, soil, temperature, light. "All the living things in an area" defines a community, not an ecosystem, and that is the most common mix-up.

Biodiversity is the number of different species in an area.

subsections.heading: Quadrats — the calculation
subsections.html:
Spec 4.2

A quadrat is a square frame of known area used to sample. You cannot count every organism in a field, so you count in several small squares and scale up.

Estimating population size from quadratspopulation = mean number per quadrat × (total area ÷ area of one quadrat)take a mean of several quadrats first · place them randomly · answer is an estimate

Three things make it valid, and each is a mark:

  • Random placement — using random number coordinates, to avoid bias. Choosing "a nice patch" invalidates the sample.
  • Enough quadrats, and take a mean — one quadrat is not representative.
  • The answer is an estimate, not a count. Say so.

To compare two areas, you sample each the same way and compare the means. A transect — a line along which quadrats are placed at intervals — is used instead when you are studying how distribution changes across a gradient, such as up a beach.

equations.name: Estimating population size from quadrats
equations.formula: population = mean number per quadrat × (total area ÷ area of one quadrat)

subsections.heading: Feeding relationships
subsections.html:
Spec 4.5 – 4.7

Food chains always start with a producer — a plant, which makes its own food by photosynthesis. Arrows show the direction of energy transfer, so they point from the eaten to the eater. Drawing them backwards is a standard lost mark.

RoleWhat it does
ProducerMakes its own food by photosynthesis
Primary consumerEats the producer — a herbivore
Secondary consumerEats the primary consumer
DecomposerBreaks down dead material — bacteria and fungi
Trophic levelThe position in a food chain

subsections.heading: Why the pyramids narrow
subsections.html:
Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level passes to the next. The other 90% is lost, and the exam wants the named routes:

  • Respiration — energy released as heat to the surroundings
  • Egestion — undigested material lost in faeces
  • Excretion — energy lost in urine
  • Not all of the organism is eaten — bones, roots

This is why food chains are short, rarely more than four or five levels: there is not enough energy left to support another level.

A pyramid of numbers counts organisms and can be an odd shape — one oak tree supporting thousands of insects gives an inverted base. A pyramid of biomass measures dry mass and is almost always a true pyramid, because mass cannot increase up the chain.

subsections.heading: Interdependence
subsections.html:
Spec 4.8, 4.9

Removing one species affects the whole community. The reasoning the exam wants runs both ways along the chain: the population of what it ate increases, and the population of what ate it decreases — and then those changes ripple onwards.

Predator–prey cycles follow from the same logic. More prey means more food for predators, so the predator population rises. More predators eat more prey, so the prey population falls. Less prey means predators starve, so predators fall, allowing prey to recover. The predator peak always comes after the prey peak.

The quadrat answer in one line

Mean per quadrat × (total area ÷ quadrat area). Place them randomly, take several, and call the result an estimate.

questions.promptHtml: A student counts daisies in ten 0.25 m² quadrats in a 200 m² field, finding a mean of 6 per quadrat. Estimate the population and state one assumption.
questions.answerHtml:
Number of quadrat-sized areas in the field = 200 ÷ 0.25 = 800.

Estimated population = 6 × 800 = 4800 daisies.

Assumption: that the daisies are evenly distributed across the field, and that the quadrats were placed randomly so the sample is representative. If the daisies were clustered in one damp corner, the estimate could be badly wrong.

questions.promptHtml: Explain why a food chain rarely has more than four or five trophic levels.
questions.answerHtml:
Only about 10% of the energy at each trophic level is transferred to the next. The remaining 90% is lost through respiration as heat, in egestion as faeces, in excretion, and in parts not eaten.

After four or five levels so little energy remains that it could not support a viable population of another organism — there would not be enough food energy to sustain their numbers.

questions.promptHtml: In the chain grass → rabbit → fox, all the foxes are removed. Predict what happens to the rabbits and the grass, and explain.
questions.answerHtml:
Rabbits increase. Their predator has gone, so fewer are eaten and more survive to reproduce.

Grass decreases. The larger rabbit population eats far more grass.

Then rabbits fall again. With the grass depleted there is not enough food, so rabbits starve and their numbers drop — the population is now limited by food rather than by predation.

Working the chain through in both directions, and then following the knock-on effect, is what separates a 3-mark answer from a 1-mark one.

questions.promptHtml: A pyramid of numbers for oak tree → caterpillar → bird is inverted at the base. Explain why, and why a pyramid of biomass would not be.
questions.answerHtml:
A pyramid of numbers counts individuals regardless of size. A single oak tree can feed thousands of caterpillars, so the producer bar is narrower than the level above it.

A pyramid of biomass measures the total dry mass at each level. One oak tree has an enormous mass — far more than all the caterpillars feeding on it — so the pyramid is the normal shape.

Biomass pyramids are almost always true pyramids because mass, unlike number, cannot increase as you go up: an organism cannot gain more mass than it consumes.

questions.promptHtml: On a predator–prey graph, the predator peak always comes slightly after the prey peak. Explain why.
questions.answerHtml:
The predators depend on the prey for food. When prey numbers rise there is more food available, so more predators survive and reproduce — but that takes time, because the young must be born and grow.

By the time the predator population has risen, the increased predation has already begun to reduce the prey numbers, which is why the prey peak has passed.

The lag is the cause-and-effect made visible: the predator population is responding to the prey population, so it must follow it.

modules.title: Food Production
modules.standfirst: The last topic on the Year 10 checklist, and the one that rewards linking back. Almost every answer here is really a photosynthesis or respiration answer wearing a farming hat.

subsections.html: Every technique here increases yield by removing something that was limiting growth. Name the limiting factor and the mark follows.

subsections.heading: Glasshouses and polytunnels
subsections.html:
Spec 5.5, 5.6

They raise yield by controlling the conditions that limit photosynthesis:

What is controlledWhy yield rises
TemperatureWarmer conditions increase the rate of photosynthesis (and of the enzymes controlling it), so more glucose is made — until the optimum
Carbon dioxideBurning paraffin heaters or adding CO₂ removes it as a limiting factor
LightArtificial lighting extends the growing day, and light is no longer limiting
Pests and diseaseEnclosure keeps pests out, so less of the crop is damaged or eaten
WaterIrrigation gives a reliable supply, needed as a raw material for photosynthesis

More photosynthesis means more glucose, which is converted to starch and cellulose for growth — so the plants grow larger and faster, and the yield is higher. That final link is worth stating; "the plants grow better" is not.

Note the limit: raising temperature only helps up to the optimum. Beyond it the enzymes controlling photosynthesis denature and the rate falls.

subsections.heading: Fertilisers
subsections.html:
Spec 5.7

Fertilisers supply mineral ions that plants need but that become depleted in soil where crops are repeatedly harvested.

IonNeeded for
NitrateMaking amino acids, and so proteins for growth
MagnesiumMaking chlorophyll
PhosphateDNA and cell membranes
PotassiumEnzymes for photosynthesis and respiration

The chain to state: fertiliser supplies nitrate → more amino acids → more protein → more growth → higher yield.

subsections.heading: Pest control — the comparison that gets asked
subsections.html:
Spec 5.8

Pests eat or damage crops, reducing yield. Two ways to control them, and the exam asks you to weigh them.

PesticidesBiological control
What it isChemicals that kill the pestIntroducing a natural predator of the pest
SpeedFast, kills most of the pest quicklySlow to take effect
Effect on other speciesMay kill harmless or useful species too, such as beesTargets the pest specifically
PersistenceCan accumulate along food chains, poisoning predatorsDoes not accumulate
RepetitionMust be reappliedPredator population is self-sustaining
ResistancePests can become resistantResistance does not develop
RiskPollutes soil and waterThe predator may become a pest itself, or eat other species

Biological control reduces the pest population rather than eliminating it — some pests must remain or the predator would have no food. That point is worth a mark on its own and is often missed.

subsections.heading: Yoghurt
subsections.html:
Spec 5.3

The bacterium is Lactobacillus. The equipment is sterilised, milk is pasteurised to kill unwanted microbes, then cooled and inoculated with the bacteria.

Lactobacillus respires anaerobically, converting the sugar lactose in the milk into lactic acid. The lactic acid lowers the pH, which makes the milk proteins coagulate — thickening it into yoghurt. The acid also preserves it, by preventing the growth of other microorganisms.

subsections.heading: The industrial fermenter
subsections.html:
Spec 5.4

A large vessel for growing microorganisms. Every feature answers the same question — why does it help the microorganisms grow?

FeatureWhy
Aseptic precautionsSterilising the vessel prevents contamination by unwanted microbes that would compete for nutrients or spoil the product
NutrientsSupply the raw materials for growth and respiration
Optimum temperatureFast enzyme activity without denaturing the enzymes
Water jacket / coolingRespiration releases heat; without cooling the temperature would rise and denature the enzymes
Optimum pHEnzymes work fastest and do not denature
OxygenationAir is bubbled in for aerobic respiration, which releases more energy for growth
AgitationA paddle stirs the mixture so microorganisms stay in contact with nutrients and oxygen, and heat is spread evenly

The cooling jacket is the one to understand rather than memorise: the microorganisms are respiring, respiration releases heat, and that heat would build up and denature their own enzymes. It is there to remove heat, not to add it.

The move that scores in every yield question

Name the limiting factor being removed, then follow it through: more photosynthesis → more glucose → more growth → higher yield. "The plants grow better" earns nothing on its own.

questions.promptHtml: A grower burns a paraffin heater in a glasshouse. Give two ways this increases the tomato yield.
questions.answerHtml:
Heat: it raises the temperature, increasing the rate of photosynthesis and of the enzymes controlling it, up to the optimum.

Carbon dioxide: burning paraffin releases CO₂, which is a raw material for photosynthesis and is often the limiting factor in a sealed glasshouse.

Both increase the rate of photosynthesis, so more glucose is made, more is converted to starch and cellulose for growth, and the yield rises.

The elegance of the paraffin heater is that one device removes two limiting factors at once.

questions.promptHtml: A farmer uses a pesticide and finds that bird populations nearby fall sharply, even though birds are not pests. Explain.
questions.answerHtml:
The pesticide is persistent — it does not break down quickly, so it stays in the bodies of the organisms that absorb it.

It passes along the food chain as each organism eats many of the level below, so the concentration accumulates and increases at each trophic level.

Birds are near the top of the chain, so they receive the highest dose, which poisons them. Their food supply may also have been reduced if the pesticide killed the insects they eat.

questions.promptHtml: Why does biological control never completely remove a pest, and why is that acceptable to a farmer?
questions.answerHtml:
The predator depends on the pest as its food source. If it ate every pest it would starve and its own population would collapse, allowing the pest to return.

Instead the two populations settle into a predator–prey cycle, with the pest held at a low level.

That is acceptable because the farmer only needs the pest population low enough that crop damage is small. The advantage over pesticides is that the control is self-sustaining — no repeated application, no resistance, and no harm to other species.

questions.promptHtml: Explain why an industrial fermenter needs a cooling jacket rather than a heater.
questions.answerHtml:
The microorganisms inside are respiring, and respiration releases heat to the surroundings. In a large vessel with billions of organisms, that heat builds up quickly.

If the temperature rose above the optimum, the microorganisms' enzymes would denature — their active sites would change shape — and growth would stop.

The cooling jacket removes the excess heat to hold the temperature at the optimum. The vessel may be warmed at the start, but once the culture is growing the problem is always too much heat, not too little.

questions.promptHtml: Describe how milk is turned into yoghurt, and explain why the yoghurt keeps longer than the milk did.
questions.answerHtml:
The equipment is sterilised and the milk is pasteurised to kill unwanted microorganisms, then cooled. Lactobacillus bacteria are added.

They respire anaerobically, converting the lactose in the milk into lactic acid. The acid lowers the pH, causing the milk proteins to coagulate and thicken the mixture into yoghurt.

Why it keeps: the low pH prevents the growth of other microorganisms, including the bacteria that would spoil the milk. The acid acts as a preservative.

modules.title: Carbon and Nitrogen Cycles
modules.standfirst: Year 10 content. Two cycles, and nearly every mark is for naming the right process or the right bacteria. Four kinds of bacteria live in the nitrogen cycle, and swapping any two of them loses the mark.

subsections.html: Atoms are never used up. Carbon and nitrogen move between the air, living things and the soil, and the same atoms go round again and again. Microorganisms do most of the returning.

subsections.heading: The carbon cycle — four processes
subsections.html:
Spec 4.10

ProcessWhat happens to carbon
PhotosynthesisPlants remove CO₂ from the air and make glucose
RespirationPlants, animals and decomposers return CO₂ to the air
FeedingCarbon compounds pass along the food chain as animals eat
DecompositionBacteria and fungi break down dead organisms and waste — and respire, releasing CO₂
CombustionBurning wood and fossil fuels returns CO₂ to the air
FossilisationDead matter that does not decay, under pressure over millions of years, becomes coal, oil and gas

Photosynthesis is the only process that takes carbon dioxide out of the air. Every other arrow puts it back. That one fact answers most "why does CO₂ rise" questions: less photosynthesis (deforestation) or more combustion.

subsections.heading: The nitrogen cycle — why plants need help
subsections.html:
Spec 4.11B

Air is 78% nitrogen, but N₂ is very unreactive, so plants cannot use it. They need nitrogen as nitrate ions to make amino acids and proteins, and they take nitrates in through their roots by active transport.

Organism or processConvertsNotes
Nitrogen-fixing bacteriaN₂ gas → nitrogen compoundsIn root nodules of legumes (peas, beans, clover) and in soil
LightningN₂ → nitratesThe energy splits the N≡N bond
DecomposersProteins in dead matter and urea → ammonia / ammoniumBacteria and fungi
Nitrifying bacteriaAmmonium → nitrites → nitratesNeed oxygen — aerobic
Denitrifying bacteriaNitrates → N₂ gasAnaerobic — thrive in waterlogged soil

The pairing that decides the waterlogging question: nitrifying bacteria need oxygen, denitrifying bacteria work without it. Waterlogged soil has no air, so nitrifying bacteria stop and denitrifying bacteria take over — nitrates are lost as nitrogen gas and the soil becomes less fertile. Ploughing and draining add air and reverse it.

subsections.heading: Why farmers grow clover and beans
subsections.html: Legumes carry nitrogen-fixing bacteria in their root nodules. Growing them, then ploughing them back into the soil, adds nitrogen compounds — a natural alternative to buying nitrate fertiliser. This is crop rotation.

The four bacteria, in order round the cycle

Fixing: N₂ in. Decomposers: protein → ammonium. Nitrifying: ammonium → nitrate, needs oxygen. Denitrifying: nitrate → N₂ out, no oxygen.

questions.promptHtml: A leaf falls to the forest floor. Trace one carbon atom in it back into the atmosphere.
questions.answerHtml:
The carbon is in organic compounds such as cellulose. Decomposers — bacteria and fungi — secrete enzymes that break these down, and absorb the products.

The decomposers use the glucose in respiration, which releases the carbon as carbon dioxide into the air. Decomposition itself does not release CO₂ — the decomposers' respiration does.

questions.promptHtml: A field floods for several weeks. Afterwards the crop grows poorly. Explain, using the nitrogen cycle.
questions.answerHtml:
Waterlogged soil has no air spaces, so it lacks oxygen.

Nitrifying bacteria need oxygen, so they stop turning ammonium into nitrates. Denitrifying bacteria are anaerobic and thrive, converting the nitrates that remain into nitrogen gas.

Both changes mean less nitrate in the soil. The crop cannot make enough amino acids and proteins, so its growth is stunted.

questions.promptHtml: Why might a farmer plant clover in a field one year and wheat the next?
questions.answerHtml:
Clover is a legume with nitrogen-fixing bacteria in its root nodules. They convert nitrogen gas into nitrogen compounds, enriching the soil.

When the clover is ploughed in, decomposers and nitrifying bacteria turn its proteins into nitrates. The wheat then has plenty of nitrate for amino acids and proteins, so less fertiliser is needed.

questions.promptHtml: Name the only process in the carbon cycle that removes CO₂ from the air, and explain why cutting down rainforest raises CO₂ in two ways.
questions.answerHtml:
Photosynthesis is the only process that removes CO₂.

Deforestation raises CO₂ because fewer trees means less photosynthesis, so less is removed; and the trees are usually burned or left to decompose, which releases the carbon stored in them.

modules.title: Human Impacts on the Environment
modules.standfirst: Year 10 content. Pollution, the greenhouse effect, eutrophication and deforestation. Eutrophication is a chain of six steps, and the marks go to people who get the bacteria using up the oxygen — not the algae.

subsections.heading: Air pollution — two gases
