Spec 4.12

PollutantSourceEffect
Sulfur dioxideBurning fossil fuels containing sulfurDissolves in rain → acid rain. Acidifies lakes so fish die, damages trees by leaching minerals from soil, corrodes limestone buildings
Carbon monoxideIncomplete combustion — not enough oxygenBinds to haemoglobin, reducing the blood's capacity to carry oxygen. Drowsiness, then death

subsections.heading: The greenhouse effect
subsections.html:
Spec 4.13 – 4.15

The Sun's radiation reaches Earth and warms it. Earth re-emits heat as infrared. Greenhouse gases absorb some of that infrared and re-radiate it back, keeping the planet warm. That is natural and necessary. The problem is the enhanced greenhouse effect: extra gases trap more heat, causing global warming.

GasMain human source
Carbon dioxideBurning fossil fuels; deforestation
MethaneCattle; rice paddy fields; landfill
Nitrous oxideFertilisers; vehicle engines
CFCsOld refrigerators and aerosols
Water vapourEvaporation — mostly natural

Consequences of global warming the mark schemes accept: climate change, ice caps melting and sea levels rising, flooding, habitat loss, species migrating or becoming extinct, more extreme weather, and changes in where crops can grow.

subsections.heading: Eutrophication — the chain
subsections.html:
Spec 4.16, 4.17

Fertiliser or untreated sewage gets into a river or lake. Then:

  1. Excess nitrates and phosphates enter the water.
  2. Algae grow rapidly — an algal bloom covers the surface.
  3. The bloom blocks light, so plants below cannot photosynthesise and die.
  4. The algae also die.
  5. Decomposers (bacteria) feed on the dead plants and algae and multiply.
  6. The bacteria respire aerobically, using up the oxygen in the water — so fish and other animals die.

Step 6 is the one that goes wrong. The oxygen is not used up by the algae, and not "because the plants stopped photosynthesising" alone — it is the respiration of the huge bacterial population. Sewage adds a second route: it is itself food for bacteria, so their respiration strips oxygen even without an algal bloom.

subsections.heading: Deforestation
subsections.html:
Spec 4.18B

EffectWhy
More CO₂ in the airLess photosynthesis, and the trees are burned or decompose
Soil erosionNo roots holding the soil, so rain washes it away
LeachingMinerals wash out of the soil into rivers instead of being taken up by trees
Disrupted water cycleLess transpiration, so less water vapour and less rain locally
Loss of biodiversityHabitats destroyed

Eutrophication in one line

Nitrates → algal bloom → blocks light → plants die → bacteria decompose them → bacteria respire → oxygen used up → fish die.

questions.promptHtml: After heavy rain, fish in a lake next to a farm die. Explain the full sequence of events.
questions.answerHtml:
Rain washes fertiliser from the fields into the lake, adding nitrates and phosphates. Algae grow rapidly and form a bloom on the surface.

The bloom blocks light from plants lower down, which cannot photosynthesise and die. Bacteria decompose the dead plants and algae and multiply rapidly.

The bacteria respire aerobically, using up the dissolved oxygen. Without oxygen, fish cannot respire and they die.

questions.promptHtml: A town switches from coal power to an anaerobic digester that burns biogas. Give one environmental benefit and one drawback.
questions.answerHtml:
Benefit: less carbon dioxide and methane released overall, so less contribution to the greenhouse effect and global warming — and less carbon monoxide, so less effect on oxygen transport in the blood.

Drawback: the Year 11 mock accepted that digesters may release more sulfur dioxide, causing acid rain that kills fish and damages trees.

The mark scheme wanted a discussion on both sides with a biological consequence for each — a gas named with no effect scores little.

questions.promptHtml: Why is the greenhouse effect necessary for life, and why is it now a problem?
questions.answerHtml:
Without greenhouse gases, the infrared radiated by Earth would escape to space and the planet would be far too cold for most life.

Human activity has increased the concentration of those gases, so more infrared is trapped. This enhanced greenhouse effect raises the average temperature, causing climate change, rising sea levels and habitat loss.

modules.standfirst: Year 11. Mitosis against meiosis is the comparison that always comes up, and the menstrual cycle needs four hormones kept straight. The January 2024 mock used a karyotype with a missing chromosome.

subsections.heading: Mitosis and meiosis

questions.promptHtml: Why must gametes be made by meiosis and not mitosis?
questions.answerHtml:
At fertilisation two gametes fuse. If each had 46 chromosomes the zygote would have 92, doubling every generation.

Meiosis halves the number to 23, so fertilisation restores the diploid number of 46. It also makes every gamete genetically different, producing variation.

questions.promptHtml: A karyotype shows 45 chromosomes with only one sex chromosome, an X. What is the person's sex, and suggest how this happened.
questions.answerHtml:
Female — there is no Y chromosome. This is Turner syndrome.

The likely cause is that the sex chromosomes failed to separate properly during meiosis, so one gamete had no sex chromosome at all. When it fused with a normal gamete carrying an X, the zygote had 45.

From the mock scheme: the ovaries do not develop normally, so there is less oestrogen, puberty and secondary sexual characteristics are delayed, and she is usually infertile.

questions.promptHtml: Explain what happens to progesterone levels if an egg is fertilised, and why that matters.
questions.answerHtml:
Progesterone levels stay high (later the placenta makes it).

Progesterone maintains the uterus lining, so the embryo can stay implanted and develop. It also inhibits FSH and LH, so no more eggs mature or are released during pregnancy.

modules.standfirst: Year 11. Both mocks had a flower question: label the parts, trace the pollen, compare insect and wind pollination. Pollination and fertilisation are different events, and the germination practical needs the right three conditions.

subsections.heading: Pollination then fertilisation
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3, 3.4

Pollination is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma. Fertilisation comes later:

  1. Pollen lands on the stigma.
  2. A pollen tube grows down the style to the ovary.
  3. The male nucleus travels down the tube into the ovule.
  4. It fuses with the female nucleus — that fusion is fertilisation.
  5. The ovule becomes the seed; the ovary becomes the fruit.

Self-pollination is anther to stigma on the same plant; cross-pollination is between two plants and gives more variation.

subsections.heading: Germination
subsections.html:
Spec 3.5, 3.6

Seeds need three conditions:

  • Water — activates enzymes that break down the food store
  • Oxygen — for aerobic respiration, releasing energy for growth
  • Warmth — a suitable temperature for the enzymes

Light is not needed — seeds live on their stored starch until the first leaves appear. The Year 11 mock explicitly refused "light for photosynthesis" as a germination condition.

The practical sets up four tubes of cress seeds: dry cotton wool (no water), moist at 20 °C (all conditions), boiled cooled water under oil (no oxygen), moist in a fridge (too cold). Only the second germinates.

subsections.heading: Asexual reproduction in plants
subsections.html:
Spec 3.7

Runners (strawberries) grow along the ground and root to form new plants. Cuttings are pieces of stem planted to grow roots. Both produce clones — genetically identical to the parent.

What becomes what

Ovule → seed. Ovary → fruit. Pollen lands on the stigma; the tube grows down the style.

questions.promptHtml: Explain why wind-pollinated flowers produce far more pollen than insect-pollinated ones.
questions.answerHtml:
Wind carries pollen randomly, so almost all of it lands nowhere useful. Producing huge amounts makes it likely that some reaches a stigma.

Insects carry pollen directly from flower to flower, so much less is wasted and less needs to be made.

questions.promptHtml: In the germination practical, why is the water in one tube boiled, cooled and covered with oil?
questions.answerHtml:
Boiling removes dissolved oxygen from the water. Cooling avoids killing the seeds with heat. The oil layer stops oxygen from the air dissolving back in.

So that tube tests whether oxygen is needed, with water and warmth still present. The seeds do not germinate because they cannot respire aerobically to release energy for growth.

questions.promptHtml: Some fruits are brightly coloured and sweet. Suggest how this helps the plant.
questions.answerHtml:
The colour attracts animals, which eat the fruit for its sugars. The seeds pass through the gut undigested and are egested far from the parent.

That disperses the seeds, so the new plants do not compete with the parent for light, water and minerals.

modules.standfirst: Year 11. The January 2024 mock asked for the genome, DNA against RNA, and the roles of RNA in making a protein — eight marks that are almost entirely named words: mRNA, tRNA, codon, anticodon, ribosome.

subsections.html:

subsections.heading: The structure of DNA
subsections.html:
Spec 3.16B

DNA is a double helix — two strands twisted together. Each strand is a chain of nucleotides, each made of a sugar (deoxyribose), a phosphate and a base.

There are four bases, and they pair by complementary base pairing: A with T, C with G. The pairs hold the two strands together. Knowing one strand lets you write the other.

Every three bases — a triplet, or codon — code for one amino acid. The order of bases decides the order of amino acids, which decides the protein.

subsections.heading: Protein synthesis — two stages
subsections.html:
Spec 3.17B, 3.18B

DNA is too large to leave the nucleus, but proteins are made at ribosomes in the cytoplasm. So the code is copied first.

Transcription (in the nucleus): the DNA unzips at the gene, and free RNA nucleotides pair with the exposed bases, forming mRNA — a copy of the code. The mRNA leaves the nucleus.

Translation (at the ribosome): the mRNA attaches to a ribosome, which reads its codons three bases at a time. tRNA molecules bring specific amino acids; each tRNA has an anticodon complementary to a codon. The amino acids are joined into a chain, which folds into the protein.

subsections.heading: Mutations
subsections.html:
Spec 3.34 – 3.36

A mutation is a rare, random change in the base sequence of DNA. It can change a codon, so a different amino acid is added, which can change the shape of the protein. An enzyme's active site may no longer fit its substrate.

Most mutations have no effect; some have a small effect; very few are significant. The rate rises with ionising radiation (UV, X-rays, gamma) and chemical mutagens such as those in tobacco smoke. Mutations are the source of new alleles.

The protein synthesis sentence

Transcription: DNA → mRNA in the nucleus. Translation: mRNA read at the ribosome, tRNA brings amino acids, anticodon matches codon.

modules.title: Selection and Evolution
modules.standfirst: Year 11. Natural selection is a five-step story that turns up in unfamiliar clothes — woodlice rolling up, fire ants resisting pesticide. The mark scheme rejects "passes on the mutation". It must be alleles.

subsections.heading: Variation
subsections.html:
Spec 3.31 – 3.33

Differences between individuals of a species come from three sources:

  • Genetic — from alleles inherited: blood group, eye colour
  • Environmental — from conditions: scars, language, a plant in shade
  • Both — genes set a potential, environment decides how much is reached: height, body mass

Genetic variation arises from mutation (new alleles), meiosis (shuffled chromosomes) and random fertilisation.

subsections.heading: Natural selection — five steps
subsections.html:
Spec 3.38

  1. A mutation produces a new allele, so there is variation in the population.
  2. Some individuals have a characteristic that gives a survival advantage in their environment.
  3. Those individuals are more likely to survive.
  4. They reproduce.
  5. They pass on the advantageous allele to their offspring, so over many generations it becomes more common.

Every step is a mark. The one lost most is the last: say alleles or genes are passed on. "Passes on the mutation" or "passes on the behaviour" was not accepted in the Year 11 mock.

Over a very long time, populations can change so much they can no longer interbreed — a new species. That is evolution.

subsections.heading: Antibiotic resistance
subsections.html:
Spec 3.39

The same five steps, fast, because bacteria reproduce every few minutes. A random mutation makes one bacterium resistant. When an antibiotic is used, the non-resistant bacteria die; the resistant one survives and reproduces, passing on the resistance allele. Soon the whole population is resistant — MRSA is the example.

Pesticide resistance works identically. In the fire ant question, numbers dropped after pesticide then rose again, because resistant ants survived and bred.

subsections.heading: Selective breeding
subsections.html:
Spec 5.10, 5.11

Here humans do the selecting:

  1. Choose parents with the desired characteristic.
  2. Breed them together.
  3. Select the offspring that show it best.
  4. Breed those, and repeat over many generations.

Examples: high-yield crops, disease-resistant wheat, cows giving more milk. The risk is inbreeding — a smaller range of alleles, so less variation, more genetic disorders, and the whole population is vulnerable to a new disease.

The five words of natural selection

Mutation → variation → survive → reproduce → pass on alleles.

subsections.html:

questions.promptHtml: Some woodlice roll into a ball when touched. Explain how this behaviour could have become common through natural selection.
questions.answerHtml:
A mutation produced an allele causing rolling-up behaviour, giving variation.

Woodlice that roll up expose only their hard shell, so they are less likely to be eaten and more likely to survive. They reproduce and pass on the allele. Over many generations the allele becomes more common, so more of the population rolls up.

questions.promptHtml: Why do doctors tell patients to finish a course of antibiotics?
questions.answerHtml:
Stopping early kills only the most susceptible bacteria, leaving the more resistant ones alive. They reproduce and pass on the alleles for resistance.

Finishing the course kills as many bacteria as possible, so fewer resistant ones survive to multiply.

modules.title: Genetic Modification and Cloning
modules.standfirst: Year 11. Two processes to learn as ordered steps: making human insulin in bacteria, and cloning Dolly the sheep. Name both enzymes in the first, and say which cell the nucleus comes from in the second.

subsections.heading: Genetic modification — making insulin
subsections.html:
Spec 5.12 – 5.15

A gene from one species is put into another, which then makes the protein. The organism is transgenic.

  1. Restriction enzymes cut the human insulin gene out of human DNA, leaving sticky ends.
  2. The same restriction enzyme cuts open a bacterial plasmid — a small ring of DNA — giving matching sticky ends.
  3. Ligase joins the gene into the plasmid.
  4. The plasmid, now a vector, is put back into a bacterium.
  5. The bacteria are grown in a fermenter; they multiply and make human insulin, which is extracted for people with diabetes.

Using the same restriction enzyme on both matters: the sticky ends only match if they were cut at the same base sequence.

subsections.heading: GM crops
subsections.html:
Spec 5.16

Crops given genes for pest resistance (they make an insecticide) or herbicide resistance, so more survive and yield rises. Concerns include genes spreading to wild plants, effects on insects that are not pests, and a smaller range of varieties.

subsections.heading: Cloning plants — micropropagation
subsections.html:
Spec 5.17B

Small pieces of a plant (explants) are placed on sterile agar containing nutrients and plant hormones. They grow into many identical plants. Used to produce large numbers of plants with desired characteristics quickly, and to save rare species.

subsections.heading: Cloning animals — Dolly the sheep
subsections.html:
Spec 5.18B, 5.19B

  1. Remove the nucleus from an egg cell (enucleate it).
  2. Take the nucleus from an adult body cell of the animal to be cloned.
  3. Insert the body-cell nucleus into the empty egg.
  4. An electric shock makes the egg divide into an embryo.
  5. Implant the embryo into the uterus of a surrogate mother.

The lamb is a clone of the animal that gave the body cell — not the egg donor and not the surrogate. Transgenic cloned animals can produce human proteins in their milk.

questions.promptHtml: Why must the same restriction enzyme cut both the human DNA and the plasmid?
questions.answerHtml:
Each restriction enzyme cuts at one specific base sequence, leaving particular sticky ends. Using the same enzyme gives the gene and the plasmid complementary sticky ends.

The bases pair up, holding the gene in place so ligase can join it into the plasmid. Different enzymes would leave ends that do not match.

questions.promptHtml: A body cell is taken from a black sheep, an egg from a white sheep, and the embryo implanted into a brown sheep. What colour is the lamb, and why?
questions.answerHtml:
Black. The lamb's DNA all comes from the nucleus inserted into the egg — from the black sheep's body cell.

The white sheep's egg had its nucleus removed, so contributes no genes. The brown surrogate only provides the uterus.
